overview.body:
**Mārs** (*mars*) ​— Father ‌of Rome · ‌The Red ​Planet — belongs ​to the ​Roman tradition, where ​it is ​catalogued under the ‌domain "War, ​Agriculture, Sovereignty". The ​name means ‌"The Roman god ​of war ‌and guardian of ​agriculture, father ‌of Rōmulus and ​Rēmus; namesake ​of the planet ​Mars and ​the month of ​March (epigraphic ‌MARS)"[^1].

Mārs ​is the god ‌the Greeks ​would not have ‌recognized. Where ​Árēs is battle-lust ‌and gets ​laughed off Olympus, ‌**Mārs is ​war as a ​Roman office ‌— disciplined, auspicious, ‌and owed ‌to the state**: ​the spear ​that stands in ‌the Regia ​and moves when ​the res ‌publica marches. But ​he is ​also the god ‌of the ​field itself — ‌of boundaries ​and crops and ​the spring ​lustration — and ​the father ‌of Rōmulus and ‌Rēmus, which ​makes him the ‌only great ​god who is ​literally Rome's ‌ancestor.[^2]

PuniCodex restores ‌the name ‌as **Mārs** and ‌serves its ​temple at [mārs.com](https://xn--mrs-1oa.com). ‌The restoration ​preserves at least ​one distinctive ​feature — a ‌diacritic or ​a distinctive ​letter — that ​the ASCII ‌form loses, and ​exactly one ​historically valid Unicode ​restoration exists, ‌which places the ​name in ‌Tier 1. The ​plain ASCII ‌form *mars* survives ​as a ‌modern convenience imposed ‌by the ​early domain-name system; ​the restoration, ​not the fallback, ​is the ‌form the project ‌defends as ​philologically complete[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested in ‌the Latin ​record — ​inscriptions and ​literature are ​the native ​sources for ‌Roman gods; ​the vowel ​quantities shown ‌are editorial ​(L&S convention). ‌Etymologically the ​name means ‌"The Roman ​god of ​war and ​guardian of ​agriculture, father ​of Rōmulus ‌and Rēmus; ​namesake of ‌the planet ​Mars and ‌the month ​of March ‌(epigraphic MARS)"[^1].

​The ASCII ‌form *mars* ​survives only ​because the ‌early domain-name ‌system could ‌not carry ​diacritics; it ​is a ‌technological compromise, ​not an ​ancient spelling. ‌The Unicode ​restoration **Mārs** ​recovers the ‌vowel length ​of the ‌original directly ​in the ​address bar. ​The restoration ​preserves at ‌least one ‌distinctive feature ​— a ‌diacritic or ​a distinctive ​letter — ‌that the ‌ASCII form ‌loses, and ‌exactly one ​historically valid ‌Unicode restoration ​exists, which ​places the ​name in ‌Tier 1.

​The letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

​- **m** ‌→ **M** ​— Same, ​capitalized
- ​**a** → ‌**ā** — ​Long vowel
‌- **r** ​→ **r** ‌— Same
​- **s** ‌→ **s** ‌— Same

​The project ​holds the ​domain **mārs.com** ​(xn--mrs-1oa.com) as ‌the canonical ‌home of ​this name[^2].

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of the ‌name is **/maːrs/** — ‌Classical Latin Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme by phoneme:

​- **M-** — Bilabial ​nasal [m] — ​the lips close ​before the name opens, ‌a held breath ​before the vowel ​that carries everything.
- ‌**-ārs** — Long ​open ā [aː] ‌— Lewis & Short ​print Mārs against ‌the genitive Mārtis ​— sustained twice a ​short a's length, ​then the rolled ​r [r] and the ​dry final s: ‌one syllable, hard ​and complete.

For ‌the modern speaker, the ​closest approximation is: ‌'MAHRS' — a ​single syllable; hold the ‌open 'ah' longer ​than English wants ‌to, let the r ​roll, and close ​it with a ‌hiss.

Kindred and historical ‌forms of the ‌name:

- **Latin** ​— Mārs, genitive Mārtis ​(Lewis & Short) ‌— the stem ​Mārt- also fathers Mārtius ​'of March' and ‌martiālis, whence 'martial.'
​- **Old Latin** — ​Māvors, the archaic ‌form the poets ​never dropped; Ovid ‌plays Mavors against Mars ​within a single ​line.
- **Greek ​rendering** — Ἄρης — ​Greek writers call ‌him by their ‌own war god's name, ​which is precisely ‌the problem: the ​translation flattens what Rome ​insisted on keeping ‌distinct.
- **Etymology** ‌— Disputed. A connection ‌to the Vedic ‌storm-deities the Maruts ​through a reconstructed *Māvort- ‌is often proposed ​but unproven; antiquity ​offered derivations from Greek ​μάχη 'battle' and ‌from mā 'male' ​with equal confidence ​and equal evidence.

Mārs ​is Tier 1 ‌because the ā ​is long — the ​quantity is guaranteed ​by the genitive ‌Mārtis and by Latin ​prosody — and ‌that single macron ​is the one feature ‌the ASCII 'mars' ​flattens. The epigraphy ‌should be stated plainly: ‌Roman inscriptions carve ​MARS with no ​length mark at all. ​The long vowel ​is restored, not ‌carved; the restoration is ‌philology doing its ​honest work.

domains.body:
Mārs is ​the god ‌the Greeks would ‌not have ​recognized. Where Árēs ​is battle-lust ​and gets laughed ​off Olympus, ​**Mārs is war ‌as a ​Roman office — ​disciplined, auspicious, ‌and owed to ​the state**: ‌the spear that ​stands in ‌the Regia and ​moves when ​the res publica ​marches. But ​he is also ​the god ‌of the ​field itself — ‌of boundaries ​and crops and ‌the spring ​lustration — and ‌the father ​of Rōmulus and ‌Rēmus, which ​makes him the ​only great ‌god who is ‌literally Rome's ‌ancestor.[^1]

### Disciplined ​War

Roman ​war under auspice ‌and command ​— the legion, ​not the ‌brawl. Mars receives ​victory owed, ​not rage indulged; ‌Cicero allows ​war only ever ‌to be ​waged to live ​in peace.

​### Guardian of ​Fields

The ‌field-god who keeps ‌boundaries and ​crops: Cato's farmers ‌purify the ​land with a ​prayer to ‌Mars before the ‌plough, and ‌the Arval Brethren ‌still dance ​for him at ‌their grove.

​### Father of ​the Twins

​By the Vestal ‌Rhea Silvia ​he fathers ​Rōmulus and Rēmus; ​the she-wolf ‌nurses them at ​the Lupercal, ​and from Romulus ​the city ‌takes both its ​king and ‌its name.

### ​Mars Ultor

‌'Mars the Avenger' ​— vowed ‌by the young ‌Octavian before ​Philippi, paid with ​the greatest ​temple of the ​age, dedicated ‌2 BC in ‌the Forum ​of Augustus.

sources.citation: Ovid, Fasti 3 (Anna Perenna, Mamurius, the Salii); Fasti 5.545–598 (the temple of Mars Ultor).

symbols.body:
The iconography ​associated with Mārs concentrates ‌in a small set ‌of recurring attributes, ​each a compressed statement ​about the name:[^1]

​- **Hasta Martis** — ​The spear of Mars ​kept in the ‌Regia at the hearth ​of the pontifex ​maximus. When Rome went ‌to war the arms ​were 'moved' — ‌the sign by which ​the whole city knew ‌the campaign had ​begun; the spear stood ​at the exact ​center of the state.
​- **Ancile** — The ​shield that fell ‌from heaven in Numa's ​reign and could ‌not stay still while ​Rome's safety hung on ‌it. The smith ​Mamurius Veturius forged eleven ‌perfect copies so ​no thief could tell ‌the true one; all ​twelve, the ancilia, ​were carried through the ‌city each March by ‌the dancing Salii.
‌- **The she-wolf** — ​The lupa who ​found the exposed twins ‌at the fig-tree of ​Rumina and suckled ​them in the cave ‌of the Lupercal. ​She is Mars's creature ​doing Mars's work — ‌his sons fed ​by his own landscape ‌— and she outlasted ​the republic on ​every coin.
- **The ​woodpecker (picus)** — ​Mars's bird, sacred above ‌others: in some accounts ‌it was the ​woodpecker that flew down ‌to feed the ​crying twins when the ​she-wolf was away, and ‌Ovid's Mavors swears ‌his oath by 'the ‌woodpecker and the wolf, ‌my birds and ​my beasts.'
- **The ‌October Horse** — ​The right-hand trace-horse of ​the winning chariot at ​the October races ‌on the Campus Martius, ​sacrificed to Mars ​on the Ides of ​October; its head was ‌fought over by ​the Subura and the ​Via Sacra, and ​its blood was kept ‌at the Regia.
- ​**The crested helmet ‌of Gradivus** — Gradivus ​— 'he who marches ‌forth,' from gradior ​— is Mars in ‌the field: the ‌god strides out before ​the army in crested ​helmet and cuirass, ​which is how the ​Forum of Augustus ‌set him in marble, ‌forty feet over the ​Avenger's temple.

sources.citation: Livy, Ab urbe condita 1.3–4 (Rhea Silvia and the twins); 6.42 (the temple in Circo, 388 BC).

mythology.body:
Mārs enters myth almost entirely as a ​father — and what he fathers is the city. His stories are ‌told by Rome's historians, not by its Homer, and they all serve ‌one thesis: **that Roman power is divine in origin and therefore answerable ​to ritual**. The Vestal and the she-wolf, the shield from heaven, the ​old king fooled at a wedding: each myth is a charter for ​a piece of the state cult.[^1]

### Rhea Silvia at the River ​(The Vestal and the Twins)

Livy opens the Roman story with a ​vestal crime that is really a divine plan (1.3–4). Numitor, rightful king ‌of Alba Longa, is deposed by his brother Amulius, who forces Numitor's daughter, ​the Vestal Rhea Silvia, into perpetual virginity so the line cannot challenge ​him. But the girl, sent to fetch water for a sacrifice, is ‌overpowered in the sacred grove by the god — or so she ​swears, 'by the god himself, she said that Mars was the author ‌of her seized virginity' — and bears twin boys. Amulius orders them ​drowned in the Tiber; the river is in flood, the basket grounds ‌at the fig-tree Ruminalis, and a she-wolf comes down from the hills ​to nurse them in the cave of the Lupercal, while a woodpecker ​flies food to the infants. The shepherd Faustulus finds them; his wife Acca ​Larentia raises them; and the twins grow up to restore Numitor and ​found a city of their own on the Palatine. Livy reports the ​whole wonder-story and then, with the honesty that makes him Rome's first ‌historian, adds that he gives it as it has come down, 'more ​adorned with poetry than burdened by proof.' The myth needs no proof: ‌it explains why the war god's temple stands at the heart of ​the city his sons built.[^2]

### Numa and the Ancile (The Shield ‌from Heaven)

In Numa's peaceful reign — the king who talked Jupiter himself ​out of human sacrifice with a handful of meal and onions — ‌a shield fell from the sky, the ancile, with a promise that ​Rome's fate hung upon it. The problem was theft: one true shield, ‌an empire to protect, and every enemy a potential thief. So the ​king set the cunning smith Mamurius Veturius a test he could not ​be told about — make eleven copies so exact that even Numa ‌could not pick the divine original — and the twelve ancilia were ‌entrusted to the Salii, the 'leapers,' priests of Mars who danced through ‌the city each March bearing the shields on their left arms and singing ​a carmen so ancient that even Augustus's scholars confessed they could barely ​construe it. The smith who made them was driven out, or stoned, ‌or honored — the versions disagree, and Ovid is visibly embarrassed by ​the tradition — but the ancilia stayed, and were still being carried ​when the empire was Christian. Mars's shield, like Rome itself, was a ‌copy indistinguishable from the original; that was the whole point.

### The ​Vow at Philippi (The Avenger)

The greatest Mars myth is not archaic ​at all — it is Augustan, and paid for in blood. After ‌Caesar's murder the nineteen-year-old Octavian marched with Antony against the Liberatores, and at ​Philippi in 42 BC Brutus and Cassius fell, one by the sword, ‌one by his own hand. Octavian had vowed a temple to Mars ​the Avenger — Mars Ultor — if he should win, and forty ​years later, in 2 BC, he dedicated it in his new Forum, ​flanked by colossal statues of the god in crested helmet, spear grounded, ​breastplate crowded with myth. The temple held the sword of the murdered ‌Caesar and the standards recovered from the Parthians — Crassus's lost eagles ‌finally retrieved by diplomacy and displayed as war won. Ovid, who was ​there, makes the dedication Rome's birthday party (Fasti 5.545–598): the new theater, the ‌games, the imperial family on the podium, and Mars's godhead finally visible ​— for until the temple rose, the Romans admitted, no image of ​Mars had any reliable claim to show what the god looked like. ‌The myth is exactly as blunt as its name: the man who ‌avenged the father became the son of a god, and Mars was ‌the instrument.

### Mars and Anna Perenna (The Old King Fooled)

Ovid ‌is the only source, and he is delighted to be it (Fasti ​3.523–710). Old Mars, he says, had fallen in love — with the ‌warlike maiden Ana Perenna? No: with Minerva herself, who with a goddess's perfect ​tact referred him onward: 'you are old; she is young' — go ​woo Anna, 'the years' own goddess.' Anna knew what the old god ​was after and, on their wedding night, wrapped herself in a veil, ‌went to the bedroom in the dark, and — had placed the ​aged crone in the bed instead. When Mars at last lifted the ​veil by the lamp's light, the laugh was heard all over heaven, ​and Anna was raised to the skies as the river of years. ‌The story is the Fasti's gift to Mars: the most ferocious of the ​gods made ridiculous by age and desire, and answered not with thunder ​but with a practical joke — Roman humor at the war god's ​expense, told in the month of his festival.

### Mars for Turnus ‌(The Enemy of Aeneas)

In Virgil's Aeneid Mars does for the losing ​side what he never does for Rome: he loves it. His favorite ‌is Turnus, the Rutulian prince who defends Italy against the Trojan landing, ​and the god moves through the last books like a pressure behind ‌the war: he sends Allecto, the Fury, to kindle the conflict in ​Book 7; he strikes Turnus with a courage beyond his own when the ‌prince pursues a phantom Aeneas onto a ship and is carried helpless ‌from the field in Book 9; and in Book 12, when the ​treaty breaks, Mars arms him for the last duel. Yet Jupiter has ​already weighed the fates, and not even the war god's advocacy moves ​the scale. Mars rages; fate is silent and exact. The scene is ​the Aeneid's quiet commentary on the god Rome trusted most: Mars can ‌arm a hero, but he cannot assign the victory — and when ‌Rome itself is at stake, the poet reminds us, the god of ​war fights on the other side too.

syncretism.body:
The interpretatio ​graeca named ‌Mars 'the ‌Roman Ares,' ​and the ​identification never ​stopped misleading ​people. Greek ​writers rendered ‌him Ἄρης ​without hesitation; ​Roman poets ‌borrowed Ares's ​mythology wholesale; yet ‌the cults ​were opposite ‌in spirit. ​Árēs owned ​almost no ​temples and ​was despised; ​Mars owned ‌some of ​Rome's greatest ‌and was ​Rome's ancestor — ‌the Salii ​danced for ‌him, the ​Arval Brethren ‌sang for ​him, and ​the old ‌Roman year ‌itself began ‌in his ​month. Outside ​the Greek ‌equation he traveled ​as a ​template: the ‌Celts poured ​their own ​gods into ‌his name, ​so that ‌Roman Britain ​knows Mars ​Camulos, Gaul ​knows Mars ​Lenus and Mars ‌Loucetius ('lightning'), ‌and Tacitus ​reports the ‌Suebi worshipping ​a Mars ​Thingsus, a ‌'Mars of ‌the assembly.' ‌The pattern ‌is interpretatio ​in its ‌purest form: ​a local deity ​kept entirely, ​a Roman ‌label laid ​over him, ​and both ​names entered ‌on the ​same altar.[^1]

​Kindred figures ​in the ‌PuniCodex cross-tradition ​index include [[ares|Árēs]] ‌(greek and ​Roman war ‌gods), [[anat|ꜥAnat]] ​(war / ‌battle), [[ashur|Aššur]] ‌(war / ​battle), [[athena|Athēnâ]] ​(war / ​battle), [[durga|Durgā]] ​(war / ‌battle), and ‌[[hachiman|Hachiman]] (war ​/ battle).

cultural-legacy.body: Mars ​is the ‌most ‌quietly ​successful name ​in ​the Western ​calendar. ​The ‌month of ​March ​— ‌Latin Martius, ​the ‌first month ​of ‌the ​old Roman ​year, ​when the ​spear ​moved ‌and the ​campaigning ‌season ​opened — ‌still ​carries him; ‌the ​weekday ‌dies Martis ​became ​French mardi, ‌Spanish ‌martes, ‌Italian martedì, ​and ​rode ‌the loan ​into ​Japanese kasei ‌and ​Korean ​hwasŏng as ‌the ​name of ‌the ​planet. ​'Martial' preserves ​the ​stem in ‌every ‌English ​court martial ‌and ​martial ​law; the ‌Campus ‌Martius, Rome's ‌field ‌of ​Mars, survives ‌as ​the name ​of ​a ‌district in ​the ​capital ​itself and ‌as ​the common ​noun ​'campus.' ‌The planet, ​blood-red ‌to every ​unaided ‌eye, ​made him ‌the ‌sky's ​permanent soldier ​long ​after the ​last ‌Salius ‌had stopped ​dancing.[^1]

sources.citation: Livy, Ab urbe condita 1.3–4 (Rhea Silvia and the twins); 6.42 (the temple in Circo, 388 BC).

archaeology.body: The ​Temple of ‌Mars ‌Ultor in ​the ​Forum ​of Augustus, ​excavated ​and partially ‌re-erected, ​held its ​colossal ‌caryatid-flanked exedrae ​and ‌fragments ​of the ‌cult ​statues; its ​dedication ​inscription (CIL ​VI ​872) survives. ‌The ​temple ‌of Mars ​in ‌Circo, vowed ​after ‌the Gallic ​capture ‌and dedicated ​in ​388 ‌BC, stood ‌in ‌the Campus ​Flaminius. ​The Regia ‌in ​the Forum ​— ‌rebuilt ​in imperial ​times ‌over archaic ​foundations ‌— housed ​the ​hasta ​Martis and ​the ‌October Horse's ‌blood. ​The Altar ‌of ​Mars and ​Venus ‌in ‌the Forum ‌Boarium, ‌vowed in ​296 ‌BC, celebrated ​the ​Julian claim ​of ‌descent. ​Roman denarii ​from ​137 BC ‌onward ​stamp the ​she-wolf ​and twins ‌on ​thousands ‌of reverses, ​and ‌imperial issues ​add ‌Mars Ultor ‌crowning ​a trophy ​— ​the ​god as ‌Rome's ‌most reliable ​mint-mark.[^1]

sources.citation: Livy, Ab urbe condita 1.3–4 (Rhea Silvia and the twins); 6.42 (the temple in Circo, 388 BC).

meditation.body:
Mārs is ​the rare ‌war god ‌who is ​also a ​farmer's god, ​and the ​combination is ​not a ‌puzzle but a ​doctrine. Roman ​war and ‌Roman agriculture ​were the ‌same activity ​at different ‌seasons: the ​boundary-stone guarded ​in peace is ​the frontier ​defended in ​war, and ‌the men ​who hold ‌the spear ​in summer ‌are the men ​who hold ‌the plough ​in spring. ‌Mars stands ​at that ​hinge — ‌Gradivus marching ‌out in ‌March, the October ​Horse thanked ​at the ‌season's close ​— and ​the state ‌that honored ​him knew ​exactly what ‌it was saying: ​that its ‌violence and ​its husbandry ​were one ​continuous act ​of possession.

‌The restoration ‌of the ​long ā is ‌a small ​act of ​the same ‌kind. The ‌inscriptions say ‌MARS; the ‌prosody says ​Mārs; Lewis ‌& Short print ​the macron ​because the ​genitive Mārtis ‌leaves no ​choice. To ​flatten the ​name to ‌'mars' is to ​lose the ​one thing ​Latin actually ‌tells us ​about how ‌it sounded ​— a ‌vowel held ​twice its length ‌before the ‌roll of ​the r, ​a syllable ​built like ​the god's ‌own discipline: ‌close, sustained, ​and complete.[^1]
